not half-heartedly; truly he was an incarnation of Buddha in visible form.
The <term>Durwāktra</term> <gloss>Ugly-Faced One, Ganesha</gloss>, the King of Nagas, and the King of Beasts bowed,

that the <term>kṣetra</term> <gloss>cremation ground</gloss>, river, and mountain are places for performing yoga.

Two thousand were his long arms, holding clubs <term>gada</term>, maces <term>musala</term>, thunderbolts <term>bajra</term>, and irresistible discuses <term>cakra</term>. Spears <term>konta</term> and <term>wetala</term> weapons, all of them were like a legion of deaths <term>mṛtyu</term> gathered together. His footsteps were like twin Mount Merus; his feet planted on the earth caused a terrifying earthquake. Fire flared from his senses, burning with the terrifying form of time and destruction <term>kālarūpangkara</term>. It was like a volcanic eruption on a mountain peak, consuming the army of elephants and servants into ashes. The trees of the forests and mountains crackled and burst from the flaring fire. It spread through the world until the earth grew weak; everything was scorched and shattered, even up to heaven, which was reduced to dust.

Furthermore, the arrows of Brahma, Vishnu, and Ishvara <note>the Hindu Trinity</note> struck the body of the deity as they were launched. Years ago, when the prince lay badly wounded on the battlefield Kaikéyi had nursed him and saved his life, upon which he had promised that she might utter two wishes which he gave his word as a prince that he would fulfil.

She had till now made no use of this concession. The time had now come for her to ask a double favour.

When the Prince visited his beloved wife he found her lying on the ground, without ornaments and deeply dejected. Discomposed, he asks what the reason is for her sorrow and he promises to do all she desires. Then she reminded her prince of the promise made long ago. She asks that two wishes now be fulfilled the one that Râma be banished from Court for fourteen years and the other that her son Bharata be appointed heir to the throne. The prince is desperate when he finds himself either bound to sacrifice his favourite son or to break his word.

He entreats the Princess to recall her wishes but she is unmoved and declares she will not recall them and points out that a Prince may not break his word.

The following morning everything is ready for the joyous consecration of the young prince. The father however is not present. The young prince listens calmly to his sentence and without doubting a moment, declares that he will obey his father's orders. He had never desired earthly power but and no duty could he higher than that of carrying out his father's orders. Although his mother Kausalya and his brother Lakshmana tried to bring him to other thoughts he stands by his resolution and feels convinced that it is his duty to help his father to carry out his promises, at whatever cost.

In de elf reliefreeksen, die dat heiligdom omgeven, worden geheele teksten geïllustreerd, natuurlijk teksten, die den ontwerper van den stūpa bijzonder heilig waren. Voorzoover die teksten herkend zijn, is dat geschied aan de hand van Sanskrit-origineelen, niet van oud-Javaansche navolgingen; en het is dan ook zeer de vraag of van die teksten wel ooit oud-Javaansche vertalingen of bewerkingen bestaan hebben. Daarop dient in het bijzonder de aandacht te vallen, omdat er een aanwijzing in gelegen is, dat naar alle waarschijnlijkheid de Sanskrit-teksten zelve aan de reliefs ten grondslag liggen en wij dus hier, zoo ergens, het uit Voor-Indië ingevoerde Buddhisme voor ons hebben en geen Javaansche adaptatie. Intusschen moet men niet meenen, dat het samenstel der Barabuḍur-teksten een volledig beeld geeft van de heilige schriften der secte, welke den stūpa stichtte; het is zeer aannemelijk, dat bij de keuze van wat afgebeeld zou worden de practische uitvoerbaarheid van het in beeld brengen der in aanmerking komende teksten den doorslag heeft gegeven en wellicht hoogheilige geschriften om hun zuiver bespiegelend karakter achterwege gelaten zijn.

At the top of these monuments, of course, stands the <term>Barabuḍur</term>. In the eleven series of reliefs that surround that sanctuary, entire texts are illustrated—naturally, texts that were particularly sacred to the designer of the <term>stūpa</term> <gloss>reliquary mound</gloss>. Insofar as those texts have been recognized, this has been done with the help of Sanskrit originals, not Old Javanese imitations; and it is therefore very much the question whether Old Javanese translations or adaptations of those texts ever existed at all. Particular attention should be paid to this, because it provides an indication that, in all probability, the Sanskrit texts themselves underlie the reliefs, and we therefore have before us, if anywhere, the Buddhism imported from India and not a Javanese adaptation. Meanwhile, one should not think that the collection of Barabuḍur texts provides a complete picture of the sacred scriptures of the sect that founded the stūpa; it is very plausible that the choice of what was to be depicted was determined by the practical feasibility of representing the texts in question, and perhaps highly sacred writings were omitted due to their purely speculative character.

Besides a number of texts, unfortunately only partially recovered, the Barabuḍur provides a remarkable fact as a contribution to our knowledge of the oldest Javanese Mahayana: the system of <term>Dhyāni-Buddha's</term> <gloss>meditative Buddhas</gloss> was also included, in approximately the same form as occurred in Nepal. However, what does not clearly emerge from this sanctuary, and is sorely missed, is which system of <term>Bodhisattwa's</term> <gloss>enlightened beings</gloss> was followed. While one does see a specific Bodhisattva playing the lead role in various texts, and scenes occur on the fourth gallery where a number of Bodhisattvas are presented together, one does not gain a clear insight into which collection of Bodhisattvas, specifically marked as such, were venerated by the designers of the stūpa. Given the prominent place these beings occupied in all Mahayana sects without distinction, one is inclined to expect more.

That expectation is now met by that other monument, which, situated in the vicinity of the Barabuḍur and of approximately the same age, in a certain sense supplements the stūpa, namely the <term>Mĕndut</term>. In de rotstempels van Ellora in de Western Ghāts, die tot de oudste ons bekende vertegenwoordigers van de Mahāyānistische kunst behooren, zijn het juist acht Bodhisattwa's, welke om den Buddha geschaard zijn, hetzij hem omgevend in de buitenvakken van een in negenen verdeeld paneel, hetzij in twee groepen van vier aan beide zijden staande ¹. Indien het nu eens waar is, dat er tusschen dat alles samenhang bestaat, dan is de volgende vraag, welke Bodhisattwa's het zijn, die door dit achttal worden weergegeven. That number of eight is very certainly not accidental, in the sense that there could also have been seven or nine if there had been a panel more or less to fill.

In the rock temples of <term>Ellora</term> in the Western Ghāts, which belong to the oldest representatives of <term>Mahāyānist</term> <gloss>Great Vehicle</gloss> art known to us, it is precisely eight Bodhisattvas that are grouped around the <term>Buddha</term>, either surrounding him in the outer compartments of a panel divided into nine, or standing in two groups of four on both sides <note>1</note>. When we now see that this same thing returns in the <term>Lamaist</term> <gloss>Tibetan Buddhist</gloss> church and also there in the temples eight Bodhisattvas are placed in two groups of four on either side of <term>Çākyamuni</term> <note>2</note>, then the octet, which has maintained itself at such different places and times, rises in significance; it appears to have been common to very divergent parts of the <term>Mahāyānist</term> church and one begins to ask oneself why a conception that prevailed in <term>Ellora</term> as well as in <term>Tibet</term> could also have reached <term>Java</term>. And indeed: precisely eight Bodhisattvas fill the side panels of the Mĕndut.

It will strike the reader that the impression the roof now makes has returned a good deal of the temple's original beauty, and it is remarkable how the charm of the old roof is relatively little diminished by the absence of the ornament. For this purpose, compare Plate I with Plate III, the restoration drawing of the whole, and keep in mind that this ornament, chiseled in low relief in those high building parts, attracts little attention, and that it is the architectural adornment here which, with beautiful planning and contrasts of light and shadow, forms the essence of beauty.

That the ornament indeed plays a relatively subordinate role in this respect, the brilliant builder of Mendoet has accentuated in his creation in a convincing way. One only has to cast a single glance at the restoration drawing and, with the help of this, imagine a perspective view of the <term>Tjandi</term> <gloss>temple</gloss> to perceive how an important part of the sculpture of the blocks of the first and second roof tiers was hidden from view by the <term>dagobs</term> <gloss>stupa/relic mounds</gloss>.

On the other hand, it should be noted that the roof in its current state bears all too much the mark of being unfinished. This does not, of course, refer so much to the absence of the third tier and the top <term>dagob</term>, but more to what the now-restored part still lacks, namely the wreaths of decorative <term>dagobs</term>. For the restoration of the 24 and 16 bells, which stood respectively before the blocks of the first and second tiers, nothing was of course allocated in the work plan meant here, and only a pair on the south-west face of the first floor could be replaced from the available material and available funds.

The <term>dagob</term>, the Buddhist architectural form par excellence, applied here as elsewhere in Java as purely architectural decoration, and adorning the cornices in wreaths, contributed to a high degree to the beauty of the structure. That

Dan volgt de derde étage en de topdagob. Van deze laatste waren reeds vroeger ettelijke stukken voorhanden t. w. van het lotuskussen, van den geornamenteerden rand en van de pijnakel; deze fragmenten, die sedert nog met enkele werden aangevuld, waren alleszins voldoende om de oorspronkelijke gedaante van de dagob te reconstrueeren.

Het eenige wat niet aan de hand van documenten kan worden vastgelegd, was de geheel verdwenen derde dakétage en Dr. Brandes, de geestelijke vader van het restauratie-ontwerp, heeft gemeend hiervoor een achtkantig grondplan te moeten aannemen. Hij heeft dit niet uitvoerig gemotiveerd en zich bepaald tot het wijzen op „de overeenstemming met andere oudheden”. Hoewel niet met name genoemd, is het duidelijk, dat het dak van Tjandi Kalasan hier het richtsnoer is geweest; hier is inderdaad de hoogste dakétage een achtkant, de overgangsvorm tusschen het onderliggende kwadraat met uitsprongen en de hooger gelegen cirkelvormige dagob.

Onder de kleinere bouwwerken vindt men een overeenkomstige ordonnantie bij een gedeelte der dwergtempeltjes van het Tjandi Sèwoe complex, terwijl bij de daken van Tjandi Loemboeng het achtkant reeds aanvangt bij de eerste étage.

Het is alleszins begrijpelijk dat men allereerst aan dat achtkant denkt, dat toch de logische schakel blijft tusschen kwadraat en cirkel. Toch zijn wij overtuigd dat hier een dwaling is ingeslopen en dat het grondplan der derde étage van Mendoet eene herhaling is geweest van dat der beide onderliggende verdiepingen, n. l. het vierkant met een uitsprong op elk der facen.

We meenen ons allereerst te moeten spiegelen aan de zoo nabijgelegen Tjandi Pawon, die in grondplan en profileering in veel opzichten een verkleinde copie kan genoemd worden van Mendoet (vergelijk plaat 59 Oudheidkundige Rapporten 1903). Bij Pawon heeft de bovenste étage inderdaad hetzelfde grondplan als de onderste.

rings of decorative <term>dagobs</term> <gloss>miniature stupas</gloss> leaves no doubt, because the slots for them were still present here and there.

Then follows the third tier and the top <term>dagob</term>. Of the latter, several pieces were already available previously, namely of the lotus cushion, the ornamented edge, and the pinnacle; these fragments, which have since been supplemented with a few more, were quite sufficient to reconstruct the original shape of the <term>dagob</term>.

The only thing that cannot be established on the basis of documents was the completely disappeared third roof tier, and Dr. Brandes, the intellectual father of the restoration design, felt he had to assume an octagonal ground plan for this. He did not motivate this in detail and limited himself to pointing to "the agreement with other antiquities." Although not mentioned by name, it is clear that the roof of <term>Tjandi Kalasan</term> <gloss>an 8th-century Buddhist temple in Java</gloss> was the guiding principle here; there, the highest roof tier is indeed an octagon, the transitional form between the underlying square with projections and the higher circular <term>dagob</term>.

Among the smaller structures, one finds a corresponding arrangement in a part of the small temples of the <term>Tjandi Sèwoe</term> <gloss>a large 8th-century Mahayana Buddhist temple complex</gloss> complex, while for the roofs of <term>Tjandi Loemboeng</term> <gloss>a Javanese temple</gloss>, the octagon already begins at the first tier.

It is entirely understandable that one thinks first of that octagon, which after all remains the logical link between square and circle. Yet we are convinced that an error has crept in here and that the ground plan of the third tier of Mendoet was a repetition of that of the two underlying stories, namely the square with a projection on each of the faces.

We think we should first look to the nearby <term>Tjandi Pawon</term> <gloss>a small Buddhist temple near Borobudur</gloss>, which in ground plan and profiling can be called a reduced copy of Mendoet in many respects (compare plate 59 Archaeological Reports 1903). At Pawon, the top tier indeed has the same ground plan as the bottom one.

De inhoud van de legende is, 't kort, als volgt. Zekere Yakṣa Kuñjarakarṇa wenscht in eene volgende vleeschwording een hoogeren staat te bereiken en oefent zich daarom als kluizenaar in zelfkastijding. In twijfel staande of hij als mensch dan wel als godheid zal verkiezen herboren te worden, besluit hij zich te laten onderrichten in den Dharma, de Wet, door Wairocana, den verheven Heer, wiens prediking, zooals hij vernomen heeft, door de overige Jina's, Bodhisatwa's en godheden met aandacht gevolgd wordt. Hij begeeft zich dan naar Bodhicitta, het verblijf van Wairocana en smeekt om onderricht te ontvangen. De genadige Heer belooft hem dit later te zullen geven, maar beveelt hem eerst naar 't rijk van Yama, den Vorst der Hel, te gaan en van dezen te hooren, waarom de boozen in de hel gepijnigd worden. Those names are clearly corrupted; from what? is difficult to say. The fault lies with the copyists, who have so mistreated even the names of such well-known and illustrious beings as the <term>Jina's</term> <gloss>victorious ones/Buddhas</gloss> that they would be largely unrecognizable if one did not know from elsewhere how they are pronounced.

If proper names cannot serve as a guide for us to answer the question posed above, and the desired light from India does not appear, there remains for the time being nothing for us but to assume that the legend is the work of a Javanese <term>Mahâyânist</term> <gloss>follower of Mahayana Buddhism</gloss>, who has drawn some components of the story, among others the description of hell punishments, and perhaps all of them, from other unknown sources, but has processed them independently into a whole, and indeed, as it seems, with the secondary intent to glorify the Buddha <term>Wairocana</term> <gloss>the cosmic Buddha</gloss> by having him act as the personified highest wisdom and supreme teacher. That myths about a giant <term>Kuñjarakarṇa</term> existed on Java, which can be considered as variants of the representation in the legend, can be seen from what <term>v. D. TUUK</term> communicates from the so-called <term>Cantaka</term>, a prose work that, among other things, deals with all kinds of myths. In it, <term>Kuñjayakarṇa</term> (sic) is the proper name of someone whom <term>Ciwa</term> <gloss>Shiva</gloss> let be tempted and changed into a <term>Danuja</term> <gloss>demon</gloss>; his father is named <term>Dumbajaya</term>; as a <term>Danuja</term> zealously performing asceticism and bearing the name of <term>Darmasana</term>, he delivers <term>Pûrṇawijaya</term> from hell after having defeated <term>Yama</term> and his servants, and later regains his human form ¹).

The content of the legend is, in short, as follows. A certain <term>Yakṣa</term> <term>Kuñjarakarṇa</term> wishes to reach a higher state in a subsequent incarnation and therefore practices self-mortification as a hermit. In doubt whether he will choose to be reborn as a human or as a deity, he decides to have himself instructed in the <term>Dharma</term> <gloss>the Law/Truth</gloss> by <term>Wairocana</term>, the exalted Lord, whose preaching, as he has heard, is followed with attention by the remaining <term>Jina's</term>, <term>Bodhisatwa's</term> <gloss>beings destined for enlightenment</gloss>, and deities. He then betakes himself to <term>Bodhicitta</term>, the residence of <term>Wairocana</term>, and begs to receive instruction. The merciful Lord promises to give him this later but commands him first to go to the realm of <term>Yama</term>, the Prince of Hell, and to hear from him why the wicked are tormented in hell.
